stimulus:
Fragments to collide with whatever comes next:

- lichen negotiating a treaty between two kingdoms
- the tide table of a harbor that no longer exists
- a ratchet that only turns when it is shaken badly
- bell-founders tuning metal by shaving its inside
- slime mold rebuilding a rail map overnight
- a ledger where every debt is paid in a different unit
- fog harvesting nets; stenciled moth wings; kintsugi seams
- an immune system forgetting on purpose
- jury selection by lottery in Athens
- a river that votes by braiding
- the sound a bridge makes before it is loaded
- sourdough starters inherited across centuries
- error as the only signal; silence as the measurement
- a map drawn at 1:1 scale, then folded
- ant bridges built from the workers themselves
- cheap noise injected deliberately into a precise instrument
- a mistranslation that turned out to be the better law
- the dead layer of a coral reef carrying the living one

Instructions to self: before answering, pick two or three fragments at random. Treat each as a hidden blueprint for a mechanism, a measurement trick, or a failure mode. Invert one assumption of the standard approach, change the scale by a factor of a thousand, or swap who the actor is. Then propose ideas that would still be testable with real data or experiments, and avoid the first three ideas that come to mind.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Shaken-ratchet pulse-history test
ideas.description: Use optogenetic or chemically gated AP-1 (e.g., FOS/JUN) activation with identical total dose but different pulse frequencies, noise levels and spacing, then measure ATAC-seq accessibility and enhancer-gene output after a washout of weeks. If AP-1 acts as a memory mechanism, the retained chromatin state should depend on pulse pattern and history rather than on total dose, and should show a threshold or ratchet-like response.

ideas.title: Acute degron removal after the stimulus (maintenance vs. initiation)
ideas.description: After a priming stimulus (e.g., inflammation, injury, or differentiation cue), deplete JUN/FOS/ATF with a dTAG or auxin degron at staggered times and measure whether primed accessibility and the faster secondary transcriptional response persist. Memory that is stored in chromatin should persist after AP-1 is removed, whereas memory that needs continuous AP-1 occupancy should decay at a rate that tracks its depletion.

ideas.title: Dead-layer footprinting: AP-1 motif sites that stay open without AP-1
ideas.description: Compare primed and naive cells by CUT&Tag/ChIP for AP-1, pioneer-like partners (e.g., BAF), H3K27ac and H3K4me1, together with ATAC and footprinting, at various times after the stimulus. Classify the sites where AP-1 binding is lost but accessibility or histone marks remain as an inherited 'scaffold' layer, then test with CRISPRi or motif mutation whether those sites cause the faster re-response.

ideas.title: Single-cell lineage-barcoded inheritance of AP-1 state
ideas.description: Combine clonal barcoding with multiome (scRNA and scATAC) sequencing and live AP-1 reporters, and compare sister cells and clones across several divisions after the stimulus. Heritability of the AP-1 accessibility state, estimated from the correlation within clones relative to random pairs, together with its decay half-life in generations rather than time, would separate true mitotic memory from persistent signaling.

ideas.title: Cheap-noise perturbation of the AP-1 circuit to map memory basins
ideas.description: Inject controlled noise (variable dose of stimulus, or tunable expression of a dominant-negative such as A-FOS) into primed cells, then quantify the bimodality and hysteresis of the AP-1 target response using flow or imaging reporters in a dose-up versus dose-down sweep. A hysteresis loop, with cells that stay in the primed basin at identical input, would show bistable self-reinforcement. Fitting the data with a model would tell us whether AP-1 positive feedback (JUN autoregulation) is sufficient or whether chromatin must be included.
